claims.feature: a world for the languages (personal aesthetic)
claims.claim: The long book was an attempt to create a world for languages that agreed with his personal aesthetic — a situation in which an Elvish greeting would be ordinary.

claims.feature: glimpses of a large history; unattainable vistas
claims.claim: Part of the attraction is the glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant city in sunlit mist; to go there destroys the magic unless new unattainable vistas open.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 247 to Colonel Worskett (20 Sept 1963)
claims.quote: unless new unattainable vistas are again revealed

claims.feature: language requires a habitation and history
claims.claim: Anyone who carries language invention far discovers that a language requires a suitable habitation and a history in which it can develop — the origin of the imaginary histories.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 294 to the Plimmers (8 Feb 1967)
claims.quote: a suitable habitation, and a history

claims.claim: The nomenclature, built from pre-existing invented languages, achieves a verisimilitude that assists literary belief in the story as historical; name-meanings are relevant solely to the fiction.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297 drafts to 'Mr Rang' (Aug 1967)
claims.quote: the ‘literary belief in the story as historical

claims.feature: Anglo-Saxon as translation device for Rohan only
claims.claim: Anglo-Saxon is used for the Mark's names and glimpses of its speech purely as a device of translation, and is the sole field for those names — delusory anywhere else.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 297

claims.claim: Tolkien objected to translating personal nomenclature and insisted the word hobbit stay unaltered; the Shire is a parody of rural England whose toponymy is not Dutch.
Shire names are not meaningless but English in form, built from elements now obsolete, dialectal, or worn-down and obscured.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings' (Nomenclature, full text)

claims.feature: euphonious names of familiar English style
claims.claim: Common-Speech renderings of Elvish names (Rivendell for Imladris) are made to be both a translation and a euphonious name of familiar English style.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: a euphonious name of familiar English style

claims.claim: Leaving such names untranslated would introduce an unexplained element with no place in the feigned linguistic history of the period — the nomenclature is a single designed scheme.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the feigned linguistic history of the period

claims.feature: hobbits adopt the style of those they meet
claims.claim: Appendix F explains varied hobbit speech by saying the more learned hobbits knew book-language and were quick to adopt the style of those they met.
claims.quote: quick to note and adopt the style

claims.feature: Appendix F cut to a third
claims.claim: The published Appendix F is only about one-third as long as its draft F2 — the visible linguistic apparatus is a deliberate reduction.

Scholars summarise the depth effect as four techniques: enormous background scale, casual incomplete mentions, multiple accounts with apparent contradictions (Red Book frame), and varying literary styles.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'

claims.feature: editorial frame (last of the philological editors)
claims.claim: Tolkien positioned himself as the last of a line of philological editors of the Red Book, so the paratexts make the text seem annotated by many hands over ages.
claims.quote: the last of a line of philological editors

claims.claim: In the Valedictory Address Tolkien says he would rather wring the juice out of a single sentence or explore one word than survey — the sentence-level craft is the method.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Tom Shippey on 'The Monsters and the Critics and other essays'
claims.quote: wring the juice out of a single sentence

claims.claim: Tolkien singularised the speech of important characters to show social and cultural differences and asked why one should refuse to use the wealth of English.
claims.source: Tolkien Estate, Ferré, Lauzon and Riggs, 'Translating Tolkien'
claims.quote: refuse to use the wealth of English

verdicts.trueWording: create a world for languages that agreed with his personal aesthetic
verdicts.note: Live tolkiengateway.net returns a Cloudflare 403; verdict formed on the raw Wayback capture https://web.archive.org/web/20260301094505id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_205. Page (Letter 205, to Christopher Tolkien, 21 Feb 1958): 'Nobody believed him, said Tolkien, when he stated that his long book was an attempt to create a world for languages that agreed with his personal aesthetic, yet it was true. An enquirer ... had been told that Tolkien wanted to create a situation in which Elen sila lumenn' omentielvo would be a common greeting.' Quote verbatim; the 'Elvish greeting would be ordinary' limb is the page's Quenya greeting = 'a common greeting'.

verdicts.trueWording: To go there is to destroy the magic, unless new unattainable vistas are again revealed
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched (1.88 MB, 493 pp) and text-extracted; letter 247 'To Colonel Worskett', 20 September 1963, PDF p. 351. 'Part of the attraction of The L.R. is, I think, due to the glimpses of a large history in the background: an attraction like that of viewing far off an unvisited island, or seeing the towers of a distant city gleaming in a sunlit mist. To go there is to destroy the magic, unless new unattainable vistas are again revealed.' Quote verbatim (the extractor injects stray intra-word spaces, e.g. 'una ttainable'; whitespace-insensitive match confirmed). Every limb supported, including the recipient and date.

verdicts.trueWording: a language requires a suitable habitation, and a history in which it can develop
verdicts.note: Same raw PDF; letter 294 'To Charlotte and Denis Plimmer', 8 February 1967, PDF p. 405. Tolkien's proposed rewording: 'The imaginary histories grew out of Tolkien's predilection for inventing languages. He discovered, as others have who carry out such inventions to any degree of completion, that a language requires a suitable habitation, and a history in which it can develop.' Quote verbatim; the 'origin of the imaginary histories' limb is the first sentence of that same passage.

verdicts.trueWording: has achieved a verisimilitude, which assists probably in the 'literary belief in the story as historical
verdicts.note: Same raw PDF; letter 297, 'Drafts for a letter to Mr Rang', dated Aug. 1967, PDF p. 411. 'this construction, the product of very considerable thought and labour, has achieved (as I hoped) a verisimilitude, which assists probably in the ‘literary belief in the story as historical.' The pre-existing-languages and name-meaning limbs are the same letter: 'the bulk of the nomenclature is constructed from these pre-existing languages, and where the resulting names have analysable meanings (as is usual) these are relevant solely to the fiction with which they are integrated.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'Anglo-Saxon' ... as a device of 'translation' ... the sole field ... entirely delusory
verdicts.note: Same raw PDF, letter 297, PDF pp. 411-412: 'The reason for using ‘Anglo-Saxon’ in the nomenclature and occasional glimpses of the language of the Eorlingas – as a device of ‘translation’ – is given in Appendix F. From which it follows that ‘Anglo-Saxon’ is not only a ‘fertile field’, but the sole field in which to look for the origin and meaning of words or names belonging to the speech of the Mark ... Outside this restricted field reference to A-S is entirely delusory.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien's most important demand was that the word hobbit stayed unaltered
verdicts.note: Live host Cloudflare-blocked; raw Wayback capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250818153124id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_190 used. Page (Letter 190 to Rayner Unwin, 3 July 1956, on Schuchart's Dutch translation): 'he objected to translations of personal nomenclature; the Shire was based on (or, as he called it himself, "a parody of") rural England; plus, the toponymy of the Shire was wholly different from that of the Netherlands' and 'Tolkien's most important demand was that the word hobbit stayed unaltered; no more "Hompen".' All four limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: not 'meaningless', but are English in form ... obsolete or dialectal, or are worn-down and obscured
verdicts.note: Raw PDF fetched from tolkien.ro (332 KB, 23 pp) and text-extracted; Guide to the Names, p. 1: 'Names (of places and persons) occur, especially in the Shire, which are not ‘meaningless’, but are English in form (that is, in theory the author’s translation of Common Speech names), containing elements that are in the current language obsolete or dialectal, or are worn-down and obscured in form. (See Appendix F.)' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: both a translation and also (to English ears) a euphonious name of familiar English style
verdicts.note: Same raw PDF, Guide to the Names p. 1: 'the author, acting as translator of Elvish names already devised ... has taken pains to produce a Common Speech name that is both a translation and also (to English ears) a euphonious name of familiar English style, even if it does not actually occur in England. Rivendell is a successful example, as a translation of Grey-elven Imladris ‘Glen of the Cleft’.' Quote verbatim; the Rivendell/Imladris limb is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: introduce an unexplained element without a place in the feigned linguistic history of the period
verdicts.note: Same raw PDF, Guide to the Names p. 1: 'to leave them unchanged would disturb the carefully devised scheme of nomenclature and introduce an unexplained element without a place in the feigned linguistic history of the period.' Quote verbatim; the 'single designed scheme' limb is the page's 'the carefully devised scheme of nomenclature'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the more learned hobbits knew book-language
verdicts.trueWording: "the more learned and able among the Hobbits" were "quick to note and adopt the style of those whom they met"
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via Special:Export (no summarizer). The quotation is verbatim and the Appendix F attribution is carried by the article's footnote (Tolkien 1955, Appendix F, 'The Languages and Peoples of the Third Age'). But the article nowhere contains 'book-language' (or 'book language' / 'bookish'): every occurrence of 'book' in the article was inspected and none supports that limb. Appendix F itself does say the learned hobbits acquired the true 'book-language', but that is not on the cited page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the visible linguistic apparatus is a deliberate reduction
verdicts.trueWording: the published version is only about one-third as long as F2
verdicts.note: Live host Cloudflare-blocked; raw Wayback capture https://web.archive.org/web/20251203174904id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/The_Appendix_on_Languages used. The quotation is verbatim: '(the published version is only about one-third as long as F2)'. The 'deliberate reduction' limb is not supported and leans the other way: the page says Christopher found it 'unknown' whether the Westron exemplifications were cut by Tolkien's judgement or 'because of the constraints on space for publication', and that 'had his father not been facing severe space constraints the form of Appendix F would have been considerably different'. The page also credits the one-third cut to the intermediate typescript F3.

verdicts.trueWording: the apparently casual and incomplete mentions of this background
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via Special:Export. All four limbs are supported: the article's numbered list of 'four factors that help to build the impression of depth' is (1) 'the enormous scale and detail of Tolkien's Middle-earth background', (2) 'the apparently casual and incomplete mentions of this background in the text', (3) 'the multiple accounts, containing gaps and inconsistencies, as if it were a real body of historical documents' (section heading 'Multiple accounts, apparent contradictions', explained via the Prologue's Red Book of Westmarch redactions), (4) 'the multiple styles in which the various texts are written, as if by different hands.' Not VERBATIM only because the supplied quotation 'casual, incomplete mentions' is not word for word: the page reads 'casual and incomplete mentions'.

verdicts.trueWording: place him not as author but as the last of a line of philological editors of ancient documents
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via Special:Export. 'Several of these contribute to his frame stories, which place him not as author but as the last of a line of philological editors of ancient documents originally written by characters such as the Hobbits Bilbo and Frodo Baggins.' Quote verbatim (the wikilink markup wraps 'philological editors' but the rendered string is continuous). Paratext limb: 'Tolkien included a mass of paratexts – prefaces, notes, and appendices of all kinds'; many-hands limb: the text 'had in that long period been annotated and edited by many hands'. 'of the Red Book' is the article's Bilbo/Frodo manuscript, named Red Book of Westmarch elsewhere in the same article.

verdicts.trueWording: rather try to wring the juice out of a single sentence, or explore the implications of one word
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched from tolkienestate.com and tag-stripped locally (no summarizer). Shippey: 'In the last text of the volume, his ‘Valedictory Address to the University of Oxford’, delivered in 1959 when he retired, Tolkien expresses his faith in literature, and gives a few clues about his method: ‘I would always rather try to wring the juice out of a single sentence, or explore the implications of one word than try to sum up a period in a lecture, or pot a poet in a paragraph’.' Quote verbatim; 'than survey' = the page's 'sum up a period in a lecture, or pot a poet in a paragraph'; 'the method' is the page's own framing ('gives a few clues about his method').

verdicts.trueWording: taking pains to singularize the speech of most of his important characters: social and cultural differences
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched from tolkienestate.com and tag-stripped locally. Ferre/Lauzon/Riggs: 'but also as a stylist, by taking pains to singularize the speech of most of his important characters: social and cultural differences are conspicuously present in the English text, from Gandalf to the Gaffer, Gollum to Theoden.' And: '‘Why deliberately ignore, refuse to use the wealth of English which leaves us a choice of styles – without any possibility of unintelligibility,’ the author wondered when a reader criticized his narrative style.' Quotation verbatim; both limbs supported (page spells it 'singularize').
